newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: France claims tide turned with EU jobs pact.
newsitem.headline: France claims tide turned with EU jobs pact.

text.p: France's divided leaders claimed a joint victory on Monday in forcing the European Union to adopt a resolution on jobs and growth they said would have equal weight with a disputed pact limiting budget deficits.

The Socialist government which swept to power unexpectedly on June 1 on a wave of anger at austerity imposed to qualify France for a single European currency proclaimed it had begun to turn the tide of EU policy.

"This is just a start, but we've only been in office for 10 days. We have started to reverse a trend. We have loosened the noose," Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's spokesman, Manuel Valls, told reporters.

He implied that Jospin's pink-red-green government had achieved more in a week since it stunned EU partners by delaying approval of the stability pact by finance ministers than conservative President Jacques Chirac had managed in two years.

Chirac, who backed the new government's call for measures to promote economic growth and employment, said the accord had been achieved thanks to "perfect coordination between the president and government".

He said the agreement contained substantial improvements on previous EU resolutions but were in line with longstanding French positions, implying that the Socialists were not alone in pushing for more action on jobs.
Chirac accepted the stability pact under intense pressure from Germany, the guardian of fiscal rectitude in Europe, at a summit in Dublin last year.
He managed to have the words "and growth" added to the title and won agreement that fines on governments that overspent limits would be subject to a political decision by EU leaders.

While Chirac suported the new government's demands, he pressed Jospin not to make good on a threat by ministers last week to delay adopting the stability pact, which limits to three percent of gross domestic product the deficits of countries that join the euro in 1999, beyond this week's Amsterdam summit.

Presidential spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said the two texts would be adopted by the summit with a single preamble which she called "a common political hat", showing the parity of importance of the jobs resolution and the stability pact.
"This does not exhaust the subject, but it consolidates what already existed and traces new paths," Colonna said.
Valls spoke of "two packages tied together with a single piece of string".

French officials stressed that for the first time, the EU's main lending arm, the European Investment Bank, would be encouraged to back innovative high-technology projects by small and medium-size businesses by taking stakes as risk capital.

The two spokespeople, who gave a joint briefing, deflected criticism that the resolution contained no financial support for job-creation programmes such as the major public works schemes which France had demanded the EU be empowered to borrow to fund.
"This opens a new stage for European integration of which we will today set the calendar and the method, with the resources coming gradually," Valls said.
He noted that leaders would consider holding a special EU summit on jobs in the autumn in Luxembourg to follow up the resolution adopted in Amsterdam.

A senior French official acknowledged that the Socialists had initially planned last Monday to hold up the stability pact, which Jospin denounced in the election as a "super-Maastricht" recipe for permanent austerity, for three weeks.

Asked what made Jospin change his mind last Tuesday, he said the angry reaction of France's EU partners, "cohabitation" with Chirac, who wanted a deal in Amsterdam, and pressure on the franc in financial markets.
